summary: UK startup Daye has added tampon-based home STI screening to its gynaecological health offerings, billing it a "world first" non-invasive service. It uses PCR testing to detect five common STIs, costs £99 in the UK, and is planned for the US and elsewhere in Europe, with HPV, GBS and herpes tests to follow. The note also covers how it works, Daye's accuracy claims, and the concern that home testing could miss opportunities such as routine HIV testing at clinics.
one_line: Daye launches a tampon-based PCR home STI test for five infections in the UK at £99, with HPV, GBS and herpes tests planned.
key_facts: Daye's "STI Diagnostic Tampon" service uses Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) testing to detect the presence of pathogens.
The service launches testing for five STIs: Chlamydia, gonorrhoea, trichomonas, mycoplasma and ureaplasma, chosen because they are the most common STIs.
Daye launched a vaginal microbiome screening service a year earlier and says it has had "thousands" of customers; it requires samples sent back with an ice pack so the lab can detect live pathogens.
The STI test is simpler because PCR looks for genetic material, dead or alive, so users only put the sample in the provided extraction solution before posting it.
Daye's signature product is a CBD-infused tampon for combating period cramps; it also sells a "nude" version without CBD.
Founder Valentina Milanova said Daye didn't invent tampon STI testing; U.K. university researchers pioneered menstrual tampon screening in the 1990s.
Daye claims test tampons collect more vaginal fluid and cover a larger surface area than swabs, making them more accurate than a swab and more comfortable than a speculum.
The STI test costs £99 in the U.K. first, with the US slated to get it "soon" and Daye working on an aftercare offering across the EU.
Users get results digitally via Daye's app in a few days after posting the sample to a partner lab.
An optional "comprehensive" nurse consultation costs an extra £29; users who test positive without buying it get a free five minute call.
HPV, linked to increased cervical cancer risk, is next on Daye's list; GBS screening for pregnant patients is coming "soon" and herpes screening later.
Daye says it lets patients book in-clinic HIV screening appointments and may expand to at-home blood testing for HIV, addressing the concern that home testing misses routine clinic HIV checks.
